entry: Tax levied on the income or profits of individuals and entities (taxpayers). It is generally computed as a tax rate times taxable income, which is usually total income less income-producing expenses and other deductions. Rates may rise with income in graduated or progressive systems, while companies are commonly taxed at a flat rate. Most jurisdictions require self-assessment and withholding on some payments, and late payers face significant penalties. For most of history, taxes were based on [[Wealth]], social position, and ownership of land and slaves. Emperor Wang Mang of the Xin dynasty established what is recorded as the first income tax in AD 9, a 10% tax on net earnings. Britain introduced a temporary income tax in 1799 to fund military efforts against Napoleon, and it later became a permanent fixture in many nations.

Male demon in folklore who appears in the dreams of women in order to seduce them. Folklore holds that repeated encounters lead to sexual intercourse and, if continued, to the woman’s declining health and death. The union is believed to produce a hybrid child called a cambion. The Late [[Latin]] word *incubus* means “a nightmare induced by a demon.” The legendary magician [[Merlin]] was said to have been fathered by an incubus. The female counterpart is the [[Succubus]]. Belief in incubi was motivated largely by distressing nighttime phenomena, chiefly wet dreams and [[Sleep paralysis]].

Men’s team representing India in international [[Cricket|cricket]]. It is governed by the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) and holds full membership of the International Cricket Council with Test, One Day International (ODI) and Twenty20 International (T20I) status. The team has played 601 Test matches, winning 187, losing 188 and drawing 225, with one tie. India won the [[Cricket World Cup|World Cup]] in 1983 and 2011 and has won the T20 World Cup a record three times, in 2007, 2024 and 2026.

Network of autonomous public engineering, technology and research universities in India. Governed by the Institutes of Technology Act, 1961, which designates them Institutes of National Importance, the 23 IITs are under the Ministry of Education and linked through the IIT Council, chaired ex officio by the Minister of Education. The first, IIT Kharagpur, was founded in May 1950 at the former Hijli Detention Camp in [[West Bengal]]. Following recommendations of the Sarkar Committee, which proposed institutions along the lines of the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), campuses were set up at Bombay (1958), Madras (1959), [[Kanpur]] (1959) and Delhi (1961). A sixth institution opened at [[Guwahati]] in 1994 under the Assam Accord. Admission to undergraduate programs is through the exceptionally competitive Joint Entrance Examination (Advanced).

Indian political party founded on December 28, 1885, also called the Congress Party. Under [[Mahatma Gandhi]] it became the principal leader of the independence movement after 1920, and it dominated Indian politics for the next 50 years after independence in 1947. Prime ministers from the party include [[Jawaharlal Nehru]], [[Indira Gandhi]], and [[Manmohan Singh]] (2004–2014). Described as sitting at the centre of the political spectrum, the party has been the main rival of the [[Bharatiya Janata Party]] since the 1990s. It won 99 seats in the 2024 Lok Sabha election, forming the official opposition.

Professional Twenty20 (T20) [[Cricket|cricket]] league in India, organized by the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI). Launched in 2007, it features ten city-based franchise teams and is held annually between March and May. It is the 11th richest sporting league in the world by revenue. In 2010 it became the first sporting event to broadcast live on [[YouTube]]. In 2023 its media rights for the next four seasons were sold for US$6.4 billion. A women’s edition, the Women’s Premier League, was established in 2022. As of 2026 there have been 19 seasons, and Royal Challengers Bengaluru won the 2026 season.

State-owned railway system of India, organized as a departmental undertaking of the Ministry of Railways. It was formed in 1951 by amalgamating 42 railway companies and manages the fourth-largest national railway system by size, with a track length of 135,207 km (84,014 mi) as of 2024. About 99.1% of its broad-gauge network was electrified by October 2025. In 2023–24 it operated 13,198 passenger trains daily, carried 6.905 billion passengers and transported 1588.06 million tonnes of freight. The first [[Steam locomotive|steam-hauled]] railway operated in Madras in 1837.

Uprising in India in 1857–58 against the rule of the British East India Company. It began on May 10, 1857, as a mutiny of sepoys in Meerut and spread to civilian revolts, chiefly in the upper Gangetic plain and central India. Rebels reached Delhi, where the 81-year-old Mughal ruler Bahadur Shah Zafar was declared Emperor of Hindustan. [[Kanpur]] was retaken by mid-July 1857 and Delhi by the end of September, and the rebellion was contained with the rebels’ defeat at Gwalior on June 20, 1858. The name is contested; it is variously called the Sepoy Mutiny or the First War of Independence. Many Indians fought for the British. The rebellion led to the dissolution of the [[East India Company]] and to direct rule under the [[British Raj]], established by the Government of India Act 1858.

Art forms of the Indian subcontinent, including painting, sculpture, pottery and textile arts such as woven silk. Geographically, it spans South Asia, including India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal and Bhutan, and at times Afghanistan, the Maldives and [[Tibet]]. The earliest art dates to prehistoric settlements of the 3rd millennium BCE, such as the [[Rock art|rock shelters]] of Bhimbetka, whose earliest paintings are some 10,000 years old. Religious traditions, including [[Hinduism]], [[Buddhism]], [[Jainism]], Sikhism and Islam, have shaped its forms. Because stone and metal sculpture, mainly religious, survived the climate better than other media, it provides most of the best remains. Indian styles spread with the religions, especially to Tibet, Southeast Asia and China, and the [[Indus Valley Civilisation]] produced thousands of small carved steatite seals.

Classical music of the Indian subcontinent, with two major traditions. North Indian Hindustani music emphasizes improvisation and exploration of all aspects of a raga, while South Indian [[Carnatic music|Carnatic]] performances tend to be short and composition-based, though the two systems share more features than differences. Both rest on the raga, a framework of notes including microtones, and the tala, a time cycle. It traditionally eschews Western classical concepts such as [[Harmony|harmony]] and [[Counterpoint|counterpoint]]. Its roots lie in the Vedic literature of [[Hinduism]] and the Natyashastra, a Sanskrit text on the performing arts by Bharata Muni. The 13th-century text Sangeeta-Ratnakara by Sarangadeva is regarded as definitive by both traditions.

Regional cooking traditions of the Indian subcontinent, shaped by religion, culture and history. Religious faiths influence the cuisines: Hindus often do not eat beef, [[Muslims]] avoid pork, and Jains are strict lacto-vegetarians. Agriculture reached the [[Indus Valley Civilisation]] around 7000 BCE, and turmeric, cardamom, black pepper and mustard were harvested by 3,000 BCE. Mughlai cuisine combined Persian and Hindu cooking, producing dishes such as pilau, biryani and kebabs. The Portuguese and British introduced baking and New World foods including tomato, potato, sweet potato, peanut and chilli, and the British introduced [[Cauliflower|cauliflower]] in 1822. Staple foods include rice and many [[Lentil|lentils]], which are often split into dal.

Series of political efforts to end British colonial rule in India, from the mid-1880s to 1947. The first nationalist movement took root with the formation of the [[Indian National Congress]] in 1885. Protests against the Partition of Bengal (1905) marked a more radical turn, which evolved into the Non-cooperation Movement (1919–1922), the Civil Disobedience Movement (1929–1931) and the Quit India Movement (1942), which demanded an end to British presence. From the 1920s [[Mahatma Gandhi]] led the movement’s adoption of non-violence and civil disobedience, though some leaders adopted violent approaches. The Rowlatt Act, which permitted indefinite detention without trial, sparked protests in [[Punjab]] that were violently suppressed in the [[Jallianwala Bagh massacre]]. The Indian Independence Act 1947 partitioned British India into the Dominion of India and the Dominion of Pakistan. The [[Constitution of India]] took effect on January 26, 1950, establishing the Republic of India.

Literature produced on the Indian subcontinent until 1947 and in the Republic of India thereafter. The Eighth Schedule to the Constitution of India recognizes 22 languages. The earliest works were orally transmitted. Sanskrit literature begins with the Rig Veda, dating to 1500–1200 BCE, and the epics [[Mahabharata]] and [[Ramayana]] were codified toward the end of the 2nd millennium BCE. Classical Sanskrit works include the plays of [[Kalidasa]], often considered the greatest playwright in Sanskrit literature. Tamil Sangam literature, the Pāli Canon, and literature in Kannada and Telugu developed in the 9th and 10th centuries. In 1913, Bengali poet [[Rabindranath Tagore]] became India’s first Nobel laureate in literature.

Philosophical traditions of the Indian subcontinent, often called *darśana*, meaning “to see” or “looking at.” Traditional classification divides the schools into āstika (orthodox) schools, which accept the Vedas as an essential source, and nāstika (heterodox) schools. The six major āstika schools are Nyāya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mīmāṃsā and [[Vedanta]]. The five major non-Vedic schools are Jain, Buddhist, Ajivika, Ajñana and Charvaka. Most share concepts such as [[Dharma]], [[Karma]] and liberation from suffering and rebirth (moksha or [[Nirvana]]). Ancient texts discuss [[Metaphysics]] and [[Epistemology|epistemology]]. Schools such as Jainism, Buddhism, Yoga and Vedanta survived, while Ajñana, Charvaka and Ajivika did not. The main schools were formalized between 500 BCE and the late centuries of the Common Era.

Land in the United States held and governed by a Native American tribal nation recognized by the federal government. Its government is autonomous but subject to regulations passed by the [[United States Congress]] and administered by the Bureau of Indian Affairs. Reservations originated from [[Treaty|treaties]] in which tribes reserved parcels of land for themselves. They cover 56,200,000 acres, about 2.3% of the country’s total area, and there are 326 Indian reservations. The largest, the [[Navajo Nation]] Reservation, is similar in size to [[West Virginia]]. Land sales under the Dawes Act left many reservations fragmented. Some permit casinos in states that do not allow gambling.

Official currency of India, subdivided into 100 paise (singular: paisa). Issuance is controlled by the Reserve Bank of India under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. Its precursor, the [[Silver|silver]] rupiya weighing 178 grains, was minted by [[Sher Shah Suri]] between 1540 and 1545 and remained in use under the [[Mughal Empire]] and British rule. The Arthashastra of [[Chanakya]] mentions silver coins as rūpyarūpa. Among the earliest issuers of paper rupees was the Bank of Hindustan (1770–1832). It is the world’s eleventh-most-traded currency as of April 2025.

Physiographic region of Asia encompassing most of the Himalayas and the land to their south, projecting into the Indian Ocean. It is politically divided among [[Bangladesh]], [[India]] and [[Pakistan]], whose territories were part of British India before partition in 1947. The term is more geophysical than [[South Asia]], which is geopolitical and also includes Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka. It was common in the British Empire and its successors. The term is increasingly less used in Pakistan and Bangladesh, where it is often perceived as offensive, while many Indian analysts prefer it for its socio-cultural commonalities.

Period of unseasonably warm, dry weather in autumn in temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. By some accounts a true Indian summer follows the first [[Frost|killing frost]]. The earliest known use in its current sense appears in a 1778 essay by J. Hector St. John de Crèvecœur. It may derive from Native American practices such as burning prairies, which produced a smoky haze. [[John James Audubon]] wrote of “that extraordinary phenomenon of North America” in his journal on November 20, 1820. Weather historian William R. Deedler defined it as “any spell of warm, quiet, hazy weather that may occur in October or November.”

State in the [[Midwestern United States]], nicknamed the Hoosier State. It borders [[Lake Michigan]] to the northwest, [[Michigan]] to the north, [[Ohio]] to the east and [[Kentucky]] to the south. Indiana was admitted to the Union as the 19th state on December 11, 1816. Its capital and largest city is [[Indianapolis]]. It is the 38th-largest state by area and the 17th-most populous. Indigenous resistance ended with the Battle of Tippecanoe in 1811 and the collapse of [[Tecumseh]]’s confederacy in 1813. The state swung from the Republican to the Democratic Party in the New Deal 1930s, but has since returned Republican majorities.

Capital and most populous city of [[Indiana]], known as “Indy.” Established in 1821 as a planned seat of state government, it is the county seat of Marion County, along the West Fork of the White River. It had 887,642 residents at the 2020 census, the 16th-most populous U.S. city and the fourth-most populous state capital. Its international reputation rests on the Indianapolis 500, held at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway and described as the world’s largest single-day sporting event. Since 1970 its government has operated under a city-county consolidation known as Unigov. Among Midwestern cities it ranks third, after [[Chicago]] and [[Columbus, Ohio]].

First inhabitants of the Americas and their descendants, including the pre-Columbian populations of North, Central and South America and the Caribbean. There are at least 1,000 Indigenous languages in use in the 21st century. Some, including Quechua, Aymara, Guaraní and Nahuatl, have millions of speakers and are recognized as official in Bolivia, Peru, Paraguay and Greenland. Pre-contact societies ranged from [[Hunter-gatherer|hunter-gatherer]] bands to city-states, chiefdoms, empires and confederacies, with knowledge of engineering, astronomy, writing and [[Metallurgy|metallurgy]]. Contact with Europeans brought epidemics of [[Smallpox]] and [[Measles]]. The term “Indian” originated with [[Christopher Columbus]], who thought he had reached the East Indies; many groups did not originally accept the term, though it has since been embraced or tolerated by many.

Primary international airport serving [[New Delhi]], the capital of India. Known as Palam Airport until 1986, it is named after [[Indira Gandhi]]. It has been India’s busiest airport by passenger traffic since 2009 and is also the busiest by cargo. In FY 2024–25 it handled over 79.2 million passengers, its highest ever. Founded by the British in 1943 as RAF Palam during the Second World War, it was later run by the Indian Air Force and then the Airports Authority of India. Since May 2006 it has been operated by Delhi International Airport Limited, a consortium led by the GMR Group.

Indian stateswoman and prime minister of India (1966–1977; 1980–1984). The daughter of [[Jawaharlal Nehru]], India’s first prime minister, she was India’s first and only female prime minister and the second female prime minister in the world, after Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Sri Lanka. She led the [[Indian National Congress]] and chaired the [[Non-Aligned Movement]] from 1983 to 1984. From 1975 to 1977 she ruled under a state of emergency, during which civil liberties were suspended and more than 100,000 opponents were imprisoned. Congress (I) won the 1980 general election in a landslide. She ordered [[Operation Blue Star]] at the [[Golden Temple]] in 1984, and she was assassinated by two of her Sikh bodyguards. Supporters cite her leadership in the 1971 war with Pakistan and the Green Revolution, while critics point to the Emergency and her authoritarian rule.

Silvery-white post-transition metal; chemical element with symbol In and atomic number 49. It is one of the softest elements, so soft that it can be cut with a knife, and its properties are intermediate between those of [[Gallium]] and thallium. Ferdinand Reich and Hieronymus Theodor Richter discovered it in 1863 by spectroscopic methods and named it for the indigo-blue line in its spectrum. Indium is used mainly in [[Flat-panel display|flat-panel displays]] as indium tin oxide (ITO), a transparent conductive coating on glass, and in [[Semiconductor|semiconductors]], low-melting solders and blue and white LEDs. It is produced as a by-product of processing other metal ores, chiefly zinc sulfide ores. Indium has no biological role, and its compounds are toxic when inhaled or injected.

Branch of the Indo-Iranian languages in the Indo-European family. With around 800 million speakers in the early 21st century, they are concentrated east of the [[Indus River]] in Pakistan, northern India, southern Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka and the Maldives, with immigrant communities in [[Europe]], [[North America]] and the [[Caribbean]]. There are in the vicinity of 200 Indo-Aryan languages. The largest by first-language speakers are Hindustani (Hindi/Urdu, c. 330 million), Bengali (242 million), Punjabi (about 150 million), Marathi (112 million) and Gujarati (60 million). Proto-Indo-Aryan was very close to Vedic Sanskrit. A 2005 estimate placed native speakers at nearly 900 million, while others suggest 1.5 billion.
